Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette: Three years ago, Thomas was attending a professional summit at the Grandview Convention Center when a deliberate electrical fire tore through the east wing. What began as a flicker rapidly became a wall of black smoke that swallowed the corridors. In the chaos, panicked attendees began hurling heavy chairs and luggage out of emergency exits to clear escape routes, the heavy thuds and sharp impacts echoing through the stairwells. Thomas found himself trapped on a landing, his lungs burning as he inhaled thick, acrid plumes of burning insulation and melting plastic. He had to push through the smoke, his vision blurring, until he finally stumbled onto the pavement, gasping. The disaster left him physically unscathed but psychologically unmoored. In the weeks that followed, the sharp tang of burnt toast from a neighbor's kitchen would freeze him in his own hallway, and watching a delivery driver casually toss a heavy package onto a porch would send his heart hammering against his ribs. These ordinary moments of sudden motion and acrid air did not simply startle him; they pulled the terror of the convention center back into his body. Rather than sit with the rising panic, Thomas immediately excused himself, retreating into isolation and shutting down any attempt to process the event. He told himself that allowing his mind to drift toward the tragedy would fracture his composure entirely, so he began systematically declining invitations from friends and refusing to engage with any shared narratives about the past. These encounters did not conjure clear pictures, but rather delivered the full, suffocating panic of that stairwell without any contextual image. Because Thomas had come to believe his own body was a liability and that mental lapses would trigger an irrecoverable breakdown, he kept the recollection locked in that detached, sensory state, never allowing it to settle into a coherent timeline. He would look at his own reflection and feel as though the terrified man in the smoke belonged to a stranger. That unprocessed, image-less recall convinced him that his nervous system was betraying him, reinforcing the conviction that he must stay hyper-alert to the next threat if he was to survive it. He now spent his days in his private counseling office, deliberately sitting with his back to the door, his posture rigid, scanning the room for any hint of smoke or sudden movement. He monitored his own internal dialogue with exhausting precision, scanning for any drift toward the event, convinced that even a momentary lapse in mental control would be catastrophic. Over months, the cycle tightened. By systematically avoiding friends and enforcing rigid thought suppression, he starved the recollection of any chance for integration, ensuring it remained trapped in that alien, unplaceable loop. His unrelenting alertness made every ordinary occurrence-a dropped pen, a whistling kettle-feel like a precursor to catastrophe. The more the memory solidified as an unplaceable terror, the more powerfully those same smells and sudden motions felt like imminent disaster, dragging the raw fear back into his awareness the moment they surfaced. Thomas realized he was no longer living in the present; he was managing a perpetual emergency. He had come to believe that the only way to stay safe was to keep his thoughts locked away and his world tightly controlled. Yet the control was fraying. He finally sought help not because the fear had lessened, but because the exhaustion of monitoring his own mind, of flinching at every discarded object and lingering scent, had left him unable to continue practicing therapy or maintaining even the bare minimum of his daily routine. He sits now in a clinician's office, hoping to learn how to quiet the alarm system that refuses to turn off, afraid that if he stops watching for danger, he will be swallowed by it all over again.
